planting.note: Plant crowns or divisions in early spring while dormant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Timperley Early is the classic English cultivar bred specifically for forcing an extra-early harvest, and like other rhubarb it needs a period of winter chilling for vigorous spring growth.

directions: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Timperley Early is a long-established English rhubarb cultivar bred and selected specifically for forcing — covering the crown in late winter with an upturned pot or forcing jar to exclude light produces exceptionally early, pale pink, sweet, tender stalks weeks ahead of an uncovered planting, a traditional practice in British kitchen gardens. Left unforced, it is simply an early-cropping, reliable garden rhubarb with slender, bright red-pink stalks and good flavor. As with all rhubarb, it performs best where winters provide real cold to satisfy its chilling requirement, so it is more reliable in temperate and upper Southern gardens than in the mild winters of the Deep South. Harvest by pulling individual stalks from the outside of the crown rather than cutting, always leaving several stalks per plant to sustain it, and never eat the leaves, which contain toxic levels of oxalic acid.

common_name: North Pole Columnar Apple (Ballerina-Series Compact Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; North Pole is a columnar Ballerina-series apple that grows as a single upright trunk with almost no lateral branching, making it well suited to a large container or tight garden space, and benefits from a second apple cultivar nearby for pollination.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; North Pole is one of the original Ballerina-series columnar apples bred in England, growing as a single narrow, upright trunk studded directly with short fruiting spurs rather than spreading lateral branches — a genetic dwarfing trait, not just a pruning technique, that lets a full-sized apple crop grow in a space barely wider than a fence post. This makes it an excellent choice for a large container, a narrow side-yard bed, or planted in a tight row as a productive, space-efficient hedge or espalier substitute. Fruit is medium-sized, red-skinned, crisp, and sweet-tart, ripening in early fall. Because columnar apples still need a genetically compatible pollinator, plant North Pole with another columnar or standard apple cultivar blooming at the same time within about 20–50 feet. Little to no pruning is needed beyond removing the occasional stray side shoot, though very light annual thinning of overcrowded spurs can improve fruit size.

common_name: Golden Sentinel Columnar Apple (Yellow Ballerina-Series Compact Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Golden Sentinel is one of the original UK-bred Ballerina-series columnar apples and benefits from a second apple cultivar blooming at the same time nearby for pollination.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Golden Sentinel is one of the original Ballerina-series columnar apples developed in England in the 1980s, growing as a single narrow, upright trunk clothed directly in short fruiting spurs rather than wide lateral branches, thanks to a natural genetic dwarfing mutation rather than grafting or pruning tricks. It bears attractive yellow-gold, crisp, sweet fruit similar in flavor to Golden Delicious, ripening in early to mid fall. The extremely narrow footprint makes it a practical choice for a large patio container, a tight side-yard planting, or a productive row spaced just 2–3 feet apart, where a standard apple tree would never fit. As with other columnar apples, plant a second compatible cultivar nearby for cross-pollination, since a single columnar apple alone sets little fruit. Prune only lightly, removing any rare side shoots that try to form, and thin crowded spurs occasionally to keep fruit size good.

common_name: Scarlet Sentinel Columnar Apple (Red Ballerina-Series Compact Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Scarlet Sentinel is the red-fruited counterpart in the Ballerina series of columnar apples and benefits from a second apple cultivar blooming at the same time nearby for pollination.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Scarlet Sentinel is the red-skinned counterpart within the Ballerina series of columnar apples, sharing the same naturally dwarfing, single-trunk growth habit as North Pole and Golden Sentinel — the tree grows as one narrow, upright stem lined directly with short fruiting spurs rather than spreading branches, staying only about 2 feet wide at full height. Fruit is crisp, juicy, and well-colored deep red, ripening in early to mid fall with good, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor. The narrow, columnar form makes it well suited to a large container, a tight side-yard bed, or a closely spaced productive row, and it can also be used as a striking, fruiting vertical accent in an ornamental edible landscape. Plant with a second compatible apple cultivar nearby for pollination, since columnar apples still require cross-pollination despite their compact size. Little pruning is needed beyond removing any stray side shoots and occasionally thinning crowded fruiting spurs.

common_name: Maypole Columnar Crabapple (Compact Flowering and Fruiting Pollinator Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Maypole is a Ballerina-series columnar crabapple grown for its showy spring flowers and small edible fruit, and doubles as a compact, long-blooming pollinator for the larger-fruited North Pole, Golden Sentinel, and Scarlet Sentinel columnar apples.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Maypole is a columnar crabapple in the Ballerina series, sharing the same narrow, single-trunk growth habit as its larger-fruited siblings while producing a spectacular flush of deep pink spring blossoms followed by small, cherry-sized, deep red crabapples that hang on the tree well into winter, valued both ornamentally and for jelly-making. Its extended, reliable bloom period makes it a useful pollinator partner for other columnar or standard apple cultivars planted nearby, extending cross-pollination coverage in a small orchard or container grouping. The narrow, upright form fits easily into a large container, tight garden bed, or closely spaced row, and needs only minimal pruning — removing occasional stray side shoots is usually all that is required to maintain the columnar shape. Small fruit can be left for winter birds or harvested for crabapple jelly once fully colored in fall.

common_name: Pix-Zee Genetic Dwarf Peach (True Dwarf Container Peach)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter or container trees any time in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Pix-Zee is a genetic dwarf — its compact size comes from the tree's own genetics rather than a dwarfing rootstock — and is self-fertile, so a single tree fruits without a pollinator.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container; Pix-Zee is a true genetic dwarf peach, meaning its compact 5–8 foot mature size is controlled by the tree's own genes rather than achieved through a dwarfing rootstock or heavy pruning — a genuinely different growth mechanism from popular container peaches like Bonanza or Bonfire that are simply naturally shorter standard-type trees. This makes Pix-Zee well suited to a large patio pot, small urban yard, or anywhere a full-sized peach tree would be impractical, while still producing normal, full-sized, freestone yellow-fleshed fruit with good sweet peach flavor. It is self-fertile, so a single tree sets fruit without a second pollinator variety nearby. Thin fruit to about 4–6 inches apart once set to improve size and prevent limb breakage, since the compact branches can be overwhelmed by a heavy crop. Provide full sun and consistent moisture, especially for container-grown trees, which dry out faster than trees planted in the ground.
